title: Beatrix and the Songbook
premise: Petra Eastwick inherited her family's failing vineyard along with a mountain of debt, and she has spent eleven years hiding from the town of Alder Creek—and from Elias Vann, the man whose heart she broke by vanishing the night before their wedding. When a contractor renovating the cellar uncovers an unsent letter Petra wrote in her grief-stricken youth, it forces both of them to confront what really happened that night: her father's blackmail, her mother's illness, and the lie Petra told to protect everyone but herself. As creditors circle and the vineyard's last harvest approaches, Petra and Elias are thrown together to save the land they both love, rekindling a romance neither can afford. In the end, Petra must choose between selling the vineyard to pay her debts or fighting for it with Elias at her side, and she finally forgives herself—marrying him not as penance, but as a woman who has stopped running.
about_author: Wendell Okafor is a former sommelier turned novelist who grew up among the orchards of the Pacific Northwest, where he learned that every family keeps one letter it never sends. He writes love stories about people who mistake duty for destiny.

chapters.title: The Weight of Empty Rows
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Opening on the eve of harvest, Petra surveys her dying vineyard and the ledger of debts her father left behind. A bank notice gives her ninety days. The emotional beat is weary resignation—she has made peace with losing everything, including any hope of a life beyond survival.

chapters.title: What the Cellar Kept
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. A renovation crew tearing out the old cellar wall finds a tin box containing an unsent letter, postmarked eleven years ago, addressed to Elias Vann. Petra recognizes her own handwriting and panics. The beat is dread—the past literally surfacing through the foundations of her present.

chapters.title: The Man Who Stayed
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias, now the town's respected vintner, learns the Eastwick property is up for sale and that Petra is back. Old anger resurfaces alongside tenderness he thought buried. The beat is conflicted longing—he wants to buy her land and confront her in the same breath.

chapters.title: Eleven Years of Silence
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Flashback chapter: the night before the wedding, her father's confession of ruin, his demand that she leave Elias to spare them both, and her mother's diagnosis. The beat is tragic understanding—readers see why Petra chose disappearance over honesty.

chapters.title: A Letter, Unopened
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra cannot bring herself to reread the letter; she burns nothing and hides everything, locking it in her desk. Her foreman Rosa urges her to face Elias before the letter does. The beat is avoidance sharpening into urgency.

chapters.title: First Harvest, Second Chance
chapters.summary: Dual POV. A regional wine competition offers prize money that could save the vineyard—but requires a collaboration entry, and the only partner available is Elias. The beat is reluctant alliance: necessity forcing two wounded people to the same table.

chapters.title: Terms of Engagement
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Elias agrees to collaborate but insists on buying the east parcel if they lose. Their negotiation crackles with old intimacy and new suspicion. The beat is guarded tension—business as armor against feeling.

chapters.title: Crush
chapters.summary: Dual POV. First days of harvest work together: stained hands, shared laughter over a broken press, muscle memory of how they once moved around each other. The beat is warmth breaking through—both realize the love never left, only went dormant.

chapters.title: The Rival Bidder
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Developer Marcus Hale makes a cash offer that would erase her debts overnight, pressuring her with a deadline that lands just after the competition. The beat is temptation—escape dangled in exchange for erasing the last of her father's world.

chapters.title: Barrels and Confessions
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Late-night tasting session turns personal; Elias asks why she left. Petra tells him a half-truth about her father's debts, omitting the blackmail. The beat is aching near-honesty—so close, yet the central lie still stands between them.

chapters.title: Rosa's Warning
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Rosa, who knew Petra's father, reveals she suspected the truth years ago and begs Petra to stop paying for his sins with her own happiness. The beat is confrontation with self—the 'person in the mirror' theme made explicit.

chapters.title: The Competition
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Their collaborative wine takes silver, not gold—not enough money to matter, but enough validation to matter more. Celebrating afterward, they almost kiss, interrupted by Marcus Hale arriving with Elias's rival bid in hand. The beat is joy ambushed by threat.

chapters.title: What Hale Knows
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Marcus reveals he's been digging: he knows about the broken engagement and hints he knows why, offering to sell the information to Elias. Elias refuses to buy gossip but can't unhear the insinuation that Petra's leaving was orchestrated. The beat is doubt taking root.

chapters.title: The Letter Read Aloud
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Alone, Petra finally rereads her own letter and weeps at who she was—young, terrified, loyal to a fault. She decides to tell Elias everything tomorrow. The beat is fragile resolve, the turning point toward truth.

chapters.title: Interrupted Truths
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Before Petra can speak, Elias confronts her with Marcus's insinuations, and the conversation detonates into accusation. Petra, cornered, says only 'ask my father'—not knowing he's beyond asking. Elias walks out. The beat is devastating setback at the worst moment.

chapters.title: Ninety Days Become Nine
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. The bank calls the loan early; Marcus tightens his deadline; the vineyard will be lost within nine days either way. Petra hits bottom, facing the mirror literally, and begins drafting the letter she should have sent eleven years ago. The beat is dark night of the soul.

chapters.title: The Mother's Archive
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Sorting her late mother's belongings, Petra finds correspondence proving her father blackmailed a business partner—Elias's father—to hide his own embezzlement, and that Elias's family lost everything covering for hers. The beat is shattering clarity: the lie protected no one and cost everyone.

chapters.title: Vineyard at Midnight
chapters.summary: Elias's POV. Unable to sleep, Elias walks the boundary line between their properties and finds Petra there, sleepless too, holding the old letter and her mother's proof. She reads both aloud under the stars. The beat is raw catharsis—truth offered without defense.

chapters.title: Forgiveness Is a Terroir
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Elias admits his own decade of bitterness blinded him; Petra asks forgiveness not for leaving but for believing she deserved invisibility. They reconcile not with a kiss but with hands in the same soil, deciding to fight Marcus together. The beat is grace—mutual absolution.

chapters.title: The Last Stand
chapters.summary: Dual POV. Climax: at the foreclosure auction, Petra publicly exposes her father's fraud using her mother's documents, clearing Elias's family name and invalidating the clouded title Marcus exploited. The townspeople, moved, rally behind a cooperative bid. The beat is courage—truth wielded as salvation, not shame.

chapters.title: Postmarked at Last
chapters.summary: Petra's POV. Petra mails the eleven-year-old letter to Elias anyway, so he can hold the words meant for the boy he was. He reads it standing in her doorway, then steps inside. The beat is tender completion—the past delivered, finally received, finally answered.

chapters.title: The Songbook
chapters.summary: Epilogue, dual POV. One year later: the vineyard thrives as a cooperative bearing both families' names. At their small wedding among the vines, Elias gifts Petra a songbook of the songs they never danced to, and they dance to all of them. The beat is joyful resolution—love chosen freely, identity reclaimed.
